title: Semicolons, colons, dashes and parentheses
blurb: Use a semicolon only between complete thoughts, a colon only after a complete thought, and dashes or parentheses to add extra information.
question: An email to new hires says, “Orientation includes: a tour, a safety class, and a badge photo, please arrive by 7:45; because parking is limited.” Which marks are wrong, and what should replace them?

teach.h: Two marks that need a full sentence
teach.body: Formally, a semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses (or separates series items that already contain commas), and a colon follows a complete independent clause to introduce a list, an explanation, an example or a quotation. Plain English: a semicolon needs a full sentence on BOTH sides; a colon needs a full sentence BEFORE it. Dashes and parentheses add extra information: dashes stress it, parentheses play it down.

teach.caption: Both marks need a complete sentence before them. Only the semicolon also needs one after.

head: Job
Example
rows: The lab closed early; the samples wait until tomorrow.
The road was icy; however, the van arrived.
Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah
teach.caption: Conjunctive adverbs: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, furthermore, otherwise, thus, instead, meanwhile.

root.label: Read only the words before the colon
root.sub: Could they stand alone as a sentence?

children.label: Colon is allowed
children.sub: Bring three items: ID, login, pen.

children.edge: No: ends in a verb, preposition or “such as”
children.label: Delete the colon
children.sub: The kit includes gauze and tape.

teach.caption: Conventional colons need no test: times (10:30), ratios (3:1), business salutations (Dear Dr. Patel:).

rows.label: The kit includes: gauze and tape.
Bring items such as: gauze and tape.

teach.caption: A pair of dashes or parentheses works like a pair of commas: open it and close it. A dash is longer than a hyphen, which joins words (well-known).

teach.body: Parentheses hold supplementary information. The main sentence's own punctuation goes OUTSIDE the closing parenthesis unless the whole sentence is inside the parentheses. Never put a comma before an opening parenthesis. Brackets are different: they mark the writer's own words inserted into a quotation (“He [the patient] refused.”).

Andre Wilson, a nursing applicant working as a unit clerk, rewrites: “Orientation has three parts: a tour, a safety class, and a badge photo. Please arrive by 7:45 because parking is limited.” “Includes:” put a colon after a verb, so he makes the clause complete first. The comma between two sentences was a splice, so he uses a period. The semicolon came before a dependent clause, so he removes it.

teach.text: TEAS favorites: a semicolon used like a comma before a dependent clause or phrase (“Because it rained; we stayed”), a colon straight after “are,” “include” or “such as,” “however” joined with only commas (a comma splice), and a comma placed before an opening parenthesis.

items: Semicolon: a complete sentence on both sides, or between series items that contain commas.
Semicolon + however/therefore + comma joins two independent clauses.
Colon: only after a complete sentence; never straight after a verb, preposition or “such as.”
Dashes emphasize; parentheses play down; both come in pairs around mid-sentence extras.
Sentence punctuation goes outside the closing parenthesis.

summary: You can now use a semicolon between independent clauses and in complex series, place a colon only after a complete clause, and choose between commas, dashes and parentheses. You can also reject the classic misuses: semicolons before fragments and colons after verbs.

A.q: Which sentence about the lab is punctuated correctly?
options: The lab closed early, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; and, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early the samples will be tested tomorrow.
A.why: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses with no conjunction.

whyNot.0: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses: this is a comma splice.
whyNot.2: A comma never follows a coordinating conjunction such as “and.”
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses with no punctuation make a run-on.

A.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly to introduce a list?
options: The kit contains: three items, gauze, tape, and gloves.
The kit contains three items; gauze, tape, and gloves.
The kit contains three items, such as: gauze, tape, and gloves.
The kit contains three items: gauze, tape, and gloves.
A.why: “The kit contains three items” is a complete independent clause, so a colon may introduce the list.

whyNot.0: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “contains.”
whyNot.1: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it; a list is not one.

A.q: Which sentence correctly joins two clauses with “however”?
options: The road was icy; however, the van arrived on time.
The road was icy, however, the van arrived on time.
The road was icy; however the van, arrived on time.
The road was icy however; the van arrived on time.
A.why: A conjunctive adverb joining two clauses takes a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

whyNot.1: “However” is not a coordinating conjunction, so commas alone create a comma splice.
whyNot.2: The comma after “van” splits the subject from its verb.
whyNot.3: The semicolon must come before “however,” not after it.

B.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates a series of cities and states?
options: The tour visits Boise, Idaho, Reno, Nevada, and Provo, Utah.
The tour visits Boise; Idaho; Reno; Nevada; and Provo; Utah.
The tour visits Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour visits: Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
B.why: When series items already contain commas, semicolons separate the items.

whyNot.0: With commas only, the reader cannot tell where each city-state item ends.
whyNot.1: Semicolons separate the items, not each city from its own state.
whyNot.3: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “visits.”

B.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: Visiting hours ended at eight; the doors were locked.
Because the visiting hours ended; the doors were locked.
Visiting hours ended; because it was eight o'clock.
Visiting hours ended at eight; locking the doors.
B.why: Both sides of the semicolon are independent clauses.

whyNot.1: “Because the visiting hours ended” is a dependent clause and cannot stand before a semicolon.
whyNot.2: “Because it was eight o'clock” is a dependent clause and cannot follow a semicolon.
whyNot.3: “Locking the doors” is a phrase, not an independent clause.

B.q: Which sentence punctuates the added information correctly?
options: Bring your ID (a driver's license or passport to the test center).
Bring your ID (a driver's license or passport.) to the test center.
Bring your ID, (a driver's license or passport) to the test center.
Bring your ID (a driver's license or passport) to the test center.
B.why: The parentheses enclose only the extra information, and no extra punctuation is added inside or before them.

whyNot.0: The closing parenthesis swallows part of the main sentence (“to the test center”).
whyNot.1: A period does not go inside a parenthetical in the middle of a sentence.
whyNot.2: A comma never goes before an opening parenthesis.

C.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: The reason for the delay was: a power outage.
One factor caused the delay: a power outage.
The delay was caused by: a power outage.
A power outage: caused the long delay.
C.why: “One factor caused the delay” is a complete clause, so a colon may introduce the explanation.

whyNot.0: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “was.”
whyNot.2: A colon cannot come straight after the preposition “by.”
whyNot.3: A colon cannot separate a subject from its verb.

C.q: Which revision correctly punctuates this sentence? “The pharmacy was out of the medication, therefore the nurse called the doctor.”
options: The pharmacy was out of the medication, therefore, the nurse called the doctor.
The pharmacy was out of the medication; therefore the nurse, called the doctor.
The pharmacy was out of the medication; therefore, the nurse called the doctor.
The pharmacy was out of the medication: therefore; the nurse called the doctor.
C.why: “Therefore” is a conjunctive adverb joining two clauses: semicolon before it, comma after it.

whyNot.0: Commas alone around “therefore” still leave a comma splice.
whyNot.1: The comma after “nurse” splits the subject from its verb.
whyNot.3: The colon and semicolon are reversed and misused; a semicolon belongs before “therefore.”

C.q: Which sentence uses a colon INCORRECTLY?
options: Bring items such as: your ID, your login, and a pen.
The orientation for all new staff begins at 10:30 on Tuesday.
One thing mattered most to the team: sleep.
The ratio of nurses to patients on the unit was 1:4.
C.why: A colon cannot follow “such as”; the words before it are not a complete clause.

whyNot.1: Colons are conventional in times such as 10:30.
whyNot.2: A complete clause comes before the colon, which introduces an explanation.
whyNot.3: Colons are conventional in ratios such as 1:4.

reteach.title: The semicolon is a balance scale
reteach.question: Picture a semicolon as a scale that only balances two equal weights, and a colon as a spotlight pointing forward. What has to sit on each side?

blocks.body: A semicolon is a scale: put a full sentence on each pan and it balances (“It rained; we stayed inside.”). Put a fragment on one pan (“Because it rained; we stayed”) and it tips over. A colon is a spotlight: a full sentence stands behind it and shines on whatever comes next (“One thing mattered: sleep.”). If no full sentence stands behind it (“The kit includes:”), nothing can switch the light on.

blocks.text: If the words before a colon end in “are,” “include,” “such as” or a preposition, the spotlight has no one behind it: delete the colon.

explain.body: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, comes before a conjunctive adverb (with a comma after it), or separates series items that contain commas. It never introduces a list and never sits next to a dependent clause.

head: Use
Example
rows: She was tired; however, she stayed.

test.q: Which sentence about the tired nurse uses a semicolon correctly?
options: The nurse, who works nights; is on call.
Although the nurse was tired; she stayed.
The nurse was tired; but stayed late.
The nurse was tired; she stayed late.
test.why: Both sides are independent clauses with their own subjects and verbs.

whyNot.0: The semicolon separates the subject from its verb and closes a comma pair incorrectly.
whyNot.1: “Although the nurse was tired” is a dependent clause.
whyNot.2: “But stayed late” has no subject, so it is not an independent clause.

explain.body: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces a list, explanation, example or quotation. Do not place it straight after a verb (are, include), a preposition, or “such as.”

rows.label: List
values: She has three: A, B, and C.
Her three are: A, B, and C.

test.q: Which sentence about favorite subjects uses a colon correctly?
options: Her favorite subjects are: biology, chemistry, and math.
Her favorite subjects include: biology, chemistry, and math.
She has three favorite subjects: biology, chemistry, and math.
She has three favorite: subjects biology, chemistry, and math.
test.why: “She has three favorite subjects” is a complete clause, so the colon may introduce the list.

whyNot.0: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “are.”
whyNot.1: A colon cannot come straight after the verb “include.”
whyNot.3: The colon splits the phrase “favorite subjects,” and the words before it are not a complete clause.

explain.body: A dash marks a sudden break or adds emphasis. A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas or parentheses but is more emphatic, and it is especially useful when the inserted part already contains commas. Do not confuse the dash with the shorter hyphen, which joins words (a well-known doctor).

rows.label: Job
values: Sets off a break or extra

test.q: Laila writes, “The kit, gauze, tape, and gloves, is ready.” The commas make the list confusing. Which punctuation should replace the two outer commas to set the list off with strong emphasis?
options: A pair of semicolons
A pair of dashes
A pair of hyphens
A colon after kit only
test.why: A pair of dashes sets off an inserted list that contains commas, and it adds emphasis.

whyNot.0: Semicolons separate independent clauses or complex series items; they cannot enclose an insertion.
whyNot.2: Hyphens join words; they do not set off phrases.
whyNot.3: A colon after “kit” would need a complete clause before it and would leave “is ready” stranded.

explain.body: Parentheses add supplementary information quietly. The main sentence's punctuation stays outside the closing parenthesis, unless an entire sentence sits inside the parentheses.

test.q: Which sentence about the test length is punctuated correctly?
options: The test lasts 209 minutes (about three and a half hours).
The test lasts 209 minutes (about three and a half hours.)
The test lasts 209 minutes, (about three and a half hours).
The test lasts (209 minutes about three and a half hours).
test.why: The parenthetical is part of a larger sentence, so the sentence's period goes outside the closing parenthesis.

whyNot.1: The period belongs to the whole sentence, so it goes outside the parenthesis.
whyNot.2: A comma never goes before an opening parenthesis.
whyNot.3: The main information (209 minutes) is trapped inside the parentheses with the aside.
